title: Why Are Dogs' Noses Actually Wet? 🐶
description:
Why are dogs' noses wet? A thin layer of mucus helps trap scent particles, licking carries them to a special scent organ in the mouth, and a 2020 study suggests a dog's cool nose may also sense faint heat.

Sources:
https://vcacanada.com/know-your-pet/why-do-dogs-have-wet-noses
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/dogs-cool-noses-may-be-able-detect-heat-180974321/
https://phys.org/news/2020-03-dogs.amp

Animated in the Low-Poly Faceted style.
pinned_comment: What's the weirdest thing your dog has ever sniffed out?
script: Your dog's wet nose traps smells you'll never notice, and it might even sense heat. That shine is a thin layer of mucus, made by tiny glands in the nose. Smells are tiny floating particles, and they stick better to damp surfaces. Then your dog licks its nose, carrying those particles into its mouth, up to a special scent organ. Dogs have over a hundred million scent receptors. You've got about six million. But here's the strange part. In twenty-twenty, scientists trained three dogs to find the warmer of two objects, from about five feet away. All three could do it. That cool nose tip may work like a tiny heat sensor, though scientists are still testing that. So what's the weirdest thing your dog's wet nose ever found?
key_facts: Glands in a dog's nose produce mucus, and a thin layer clings to the nostrils and helps absorb scent chemicals (VCA)
Scent particles stick better to damp surfaces (VCA)
Dogs lick their noses, carrying scent particles to the Jacobson's organ on the roof of the mouth (VCA)
Dogs have more than 100 million scent receptor sites, humans about 6 million (VCA, Smithsonian)
In a 2020 Scientific Reports study, three trained dogs picked the warmer of two objects from about 1.6 m / five feet (Smithsonian, Phys.org)
Brain scans of 13 dogs showed the somatosensory cortex responding to weak heat; whether the nose tip is the sensor is not yet proven (Smithsonian, Phys.org)
